paras.text: Contractors, Liens and Assignment of Benefits in Claims, Audio Lecture
Three bodies of Michigan law collide inside a single restoration job.

The Construction Lien Act, which governs how a contractor gets paid by the homeowner. The Insurance Code, which governs the homeowner's claim against the carrier. And old fashioned assignment law, which governs whether the contractor can step into the homeowner's shoes and deal with the carrier directly.

Get any one of these wrong and the contractor can do excellent work and collect nothing for it. That is not a figure of speech. In the first case we are going to cover, a man did the work and ended up with nothing but exposure.
So this is the chapter where the law touches your actual business hardest. Fourteen ideas. After most of them, a question and then silence. Answer out loud.
Idea one. Epps, and the facts worth picturing.
The case that anchors this whole chapter is Epps versus four Quarters Restoration, four ninety eight Michigan five eighteen, decided in twenty fifteen.

A home in Detroit floods in two thousand six. The homeowners, Danny and Joyce Epps, are referred to a man named Troy Willis and his companies, four Quarters Restoration and Emergency Insurance Services.
Willis is not a licensed residential builder when he does the work. His builder's license had been revoked on January thirty first of two thousand six, and he did not tell the Epps that.

The Epps sign a repair agreement assigning the insurance proceeds to Willis's company. Willis went on to receive and endorse Auto Owners checks totaling one hundred twenty eight thousand and forty seven dollars, signing the Epps' names himself.
If that sounds like a modern assignment of benefits arrangement, that is because it basically is one. Which is exactly why this case sits at the front of the chapter.
Idea two. Void or voidable, and the word doing the work.

The Michigan Supreme Court had to answer a basic sounding question. Is a contract with an unlicensed builder void, meaning it never legally existed, or voidable, meaning it is valid unless and until someone chooses to void it?
The difference is enormous. If void, neither side has any rights under it at all.
The Court held that contracts between an innocent homeowner and an unlicensed residential builder are voidable, not void, correcting sloppier language in older opinions.
Now here is the nuance that most summaries of this case get wrong, and it is worth slowing down for.

The word innocent in that holding is not decorative. The Michigan Supreme Court expressly limited its ruling to a homeowner who did not know the contractor was unlicensed. In the Epps' own case, there was no indication in the record that they knew Willis was unlicensed, so the Court said its analysis was limited to that fact pattern.
The Court did not decide what happens if a homeowner knowingly hires an unlicensed contractor.

So if you ever hear someone say Epps means the voidable rule applies no matter what the homeowner knew, that is an overstatement of the actual holding. Say the narrower version. It is the one that is true.
Idea three. The suit bar, which does not care what anybody knew.
There is a second piece of Epps that is completely separate from the void versus voidable question, and this one genuinely does not care what the homeowner knew.

The statute at issue, M C L three thirty nine point twenty four twelve, subsection one, says an unlicensed contractor cannot bring or maintain a lawsuit to collect compensation without alleging and proving it was licensed during performance.
No knowledge exception anywhere in the text. None.

The Michigan Supreme Court described this rule using a phrase borrowed from an earlier Court of Appeals case, Parker versus McQuade Plumbing and Heating. The statute operates as a shield, not a sword.

Unpack that phrase, because it is precise. It removes the unlicensed contractor's power to sue. It does not remove the contractor's power to defend itself if the homeowner sues first. And it does not hand the homeowner an independent right to sue the unlicensed contractor to get money back. The Court specifically declined to read that private right of action into the statute.

So hold the two part structure of Epps in your head as two separate things. The suit bar under subsection one is absolute and knowledge independent. The void versus voidable classification of the contract itself was decided only for the innocent homeowner scenario.
Question. Unlicensed contractor, homeowner refuses to pay. Can he sue? Can he defend if she sues him? Can she sue him just for being unlicensed?

He cannot sue, because subsection one bars it with no knowledge exception. He can defend himself if she sues first, because it is a shield not a sword. And she has no independent private right of action just for the unlicensed status, because the Court declined to read one in.
Idea four. The rest of twenty four twelve.
That same statute, subsection three, also says an unlicensed contractor cannot impose a construction lien on the property.
And subsection four lets a prosecutor or the attorney general sue for a civil fine of not less than five thousand and not more than twenty five thousand dollars.
Put it together. No lawsuit, no lien, and a fine between five and twenty five thousand dollars. Licensing is not a technicality. It is the foundation everything else in this chapter sits on.
Idea five. The written contract rule that kills liens.
Now the Construction Lien Act rules for residential work, because a restoration job is almost always residential.

M C L five seventy point eleven fourteen says a contractor has no right to a construction lien on a homeowner's property unless the improvement was done under a written contract, with any amendments also in writing, and that contract states, in type no smaller than the body of the contract, that the work requires a license and, if it does, that the contractor is licensed and the actual license number.
Three details there that people miss.
There is no dollar floor. This is not a rule that kicks in above some threshold. It applies to residential work, period.
The type size requirement is real. No smaller than the body of the contract.

And this is the one that costs money: miss the license number and the lien is gone, even if the contractor is genuinely licensed. A fully licensed contractor with a perfect job loses lien rights over a missing number on a page.
Question. Licensed contractor, written contract, amendments in writing, but the license number was never typed in. Does he have a lien?
No. Under five seventy point eleven fourteen the contract has to state the actual license number. Being genuinely licensed does not save the lien.
Idea six. Three clocks, plus one for laborers.
You need these cold, so let me give them as a chain.
Twenty days. A subcontractor or supplier has to serve a Notice of Furnishing within twenty days after furnishing the first labor or material, under M C L five seventy point eleven zero nine.

But here is a favorite trap. A contractor in direct contract with the homeowner does not have to serve this notice at all. The twenty day clock is for subs and suppliers, not the general contractor dealing straight with the owner.

Ninety days. Under M C L five seventy point eleven eleven, the right to a construction lien ceases to exist unless a claim of lien is recorded with the register of deeds within ninety days after the lien claimant's last furnishing of labor or material. That is a hard, absolute deadline.
One year. Under M C L five seventy point eleven seventeen, once you have recorded that claim of lien, you have to file suit to foreclose it within one year of the recording date, or the lien expires.
And one more to keep separate. A laborer, as opposed to a subcontractor or supplier, gets thirty days after wages were due but unpaid, under subsection two of eleven zero nine.
Twenty, ninety, one year. And thirty for a laborer. Notice that ninety runs from last furnishing, while the one year runs from recording. Two different starting guns.
Question. Last day of work was August first. What is your recording deadline, and once you record on October twentieth, what is your next deadline?
Ninety days from August first, so roughly October thirtieth, to record the claim of lien. Then one year from the October twentieth recording date to file suit to foreclose.
Idea seven. The sworn statement.
Layered on top is M C L five seventy point eleven ten, the sworn statement rule.
A contractor has to give the owner a sworn statement listing every sub, supplier, and unpaid laborer whenever payment is due, requested, or demanded.
Note all three triggers. Due, requested, or demanded. Any one of them.
And lie on it with intent to defraud, and that is a crime. Not a contract dispute. A crime.
Idea eight. Assignment of benefits, and a case from eighteen eighty.
Now the assignment question, because this is where most of the confusion in a restoration practice actually lives.
Start with something surprising. Michigan has never passed a statute specifically regulating assignment of benefits for property insurance. There is no A O B statute here at all.
The entire doctrine is common law, and it goes all the way back to eighteen eighty.

The case is Roger Williams Insurance Company versus Carrington, forty three Michigan two fifty two. A livery stable's fire insurance policy covered property that burned down. After the fire, the insured assigned the policy to secure a debt, without asking the insurance company's permission. The company said the policy's anti assignment clause voided the whole thing.

The Michigan Supreme Court disagreed, and the language it used is still quoted by Michigan courts today. The assignment, having been made after the loss, did not require the company's consent, and a policy provision forfeiting coverage for an unconsented assignment is invalid as applied to the transfer of an already accrued claim.
The Court called it the absolute right of every person to assign such a claim, and said preventing that right would be against public policy.

Hear the logic, because it is clean. Before the loss, the carrier cares enormously who it is insuring. After the loss, the claim is just a debt, a fixed sum owed, and you can assign a debt. The identity of the person holding it does not change the carrier's risk at all.
Idea nine. Shah, the modern restatement, and its limits.
That rule got a modern restatement in twenty eighteen, in Jawad A. Shah, M.D., P C, versus State Farm, three twenty four Michigan Appeals one eighty two.

Label it right: this is a no fault case, not a property case. But healthcare providers had taken an assignment of a patient's no fault benefits after treating him, and the Court of Appeals leaned directly on Roger Williams to reach the same result.

State Farm's policy said no assignment of benefits was binding without its approval. The Court held that clause unenforceable, because the assignment here was of an accrued claim, made after the loss, for services already provided.

And the Court was careful about the reasoning, in a way you should copy. This is not about the clause being unreasonable. Michigan generally enforces clear contract language as written under Rory versus Continental. This is narrower: enforcing an anti assignment clause against a genuinely post loss transfer of an accrued claim violates the same public policy identified in eighteen eighty.
So for your restoration practice, here is the usable rule. If a homeowner signs an assignment of benefits for work already done, an anti assignment clause in her policy cannot block it.

But that protection is narrow, and the two limits matter more than the rule. It does not extend to a pre loss transfer of the policy itself. And it says nothing about whether the contractor can act as the adjuster once it has the assignment.
That is a separate question, and the answer to it is no.
Idea ten. What an assignment does not give you.
Here is where a lot of restoration companies get themselves in real trouble, so let me be exact.
An assignment of benefits gives a contractor standing to sue the carrier as an assignee, stepping into the homeowner's contractual shoes for the assigned, accrued claim.
It does not create any new rights the homeowner did not already have. An assignee inherits the claim as it was, not a better version of it.
And it does not license the contractor to negotiate or adjust the claim.

M C L five hundred point twelve twenty two says a person cannot adjust loss or damage under a policy, or hold themselves out as an adjuster, without a license, with exactly five exemptions. Michigan attorneys. Marine average adjusters. An insurer's own employees. A licensed producer with granted claim authority. And a narrow supervised data entry role.
A restoration contractor is not on that list. Assignment or not. Holding a piece of paper from the homeowner does not add a sixth exemption to a statute that has five.
Question. You hold a signed post loss assignment of benefits. What does it let you do, and what does it not let you do?

It lets you stand in the homeowner's shoes to pursue the accrued claim, including suing the carrier as assignee, and an anti assignment clause cannot block it. It does not give you any new rights she did not have, and it does not let you adjust or negotiate the claim, because twelve twenty two has five exemptions and contractor is not one.
Idea eleven. Guldshtadt, where that line got crossed.
This is exactly the mistake that got a real Michigan adjuster in real trouble.

D I F S case number twenty five, dash, one eight three five zero, involves an adjuster named Aleksandr Guldshtadt. He was summarily suspended in November of twenty twenty five, and the final decision issued April first of twenty twenty six revoked his license outright and ordered him to pay a fifty thousand dollar civil fine.

Look at the pattern of conduct, because it reads like a checklist of this chapter. He held a financial interest in a fire repair contractor. He used adjusting contracts D I F S had never approved. He let unlicensed people sign consumers up. And he diverted claim money to a contracting business he had an interest in.
D I F S charged that under M C L five hundred point twelve twenty six, and reached his license through twelve twenty four, subsection three, plus twelve forty two, subsection two.
Separately, subsection four of twelve twenty four is the flat rule that a person connected with a fire repair contractor cannot be issued an adjuster license at all.

Now draw the line to your own business, because this is the sentence to remember. A restoration company with an assignment of benefits that negotiates a disputed scope for a percentage fee is walking that exact same line.
Idea twelve. The twelve percent, and an honest unknown.

M C L five hundred point two thousand six, subsection four, says an insurer owes twelve percent simple interest on a late paid claim, belonging to the insured or a person directly entitled to benefits.

Now the honest part. No published Michigan property insurance case has decided whether a contractor holding an assignment of benefits counts as a person directly entitled to benefits in its own right.
So do not promise that twelve percent as an automatic entitlement for the contractor. If you tell a homeowner or a partner that, you are stating as settled something no Michigan court has settled.
Here is the honest framing that is still useful. The contractor pursues it derivatively, standing in the homeowner's shoes, because the homeowner's own right survives the assignment.
That is meaningfully different from claiming the contractor owns the twelve percent outright, and the difference is the kind of thing that gets noticed in a deposition.
Idea thirteen. The Consumer Protection Act, and why it almost never works.
People reach for this constantly when frustrated with a carrier, and it almost never works.
The general exemption is M C L four forty five point nine zero four, subsection one, letter A. The act does not apply to conduct specifically authorized under laws administered by a regulatory board.

The case usually cited here is Smith versus Globe Life Insurance Company, four sixty Michigan four forty six, from nineteen ninety nine. But that case is usually oversimplified, and you should know why.

In nineteen ninety nine, the version of the statute then in force had a carve out permitting certain private actions for chapter twenty insurance code conduct, and that is specifically why the plaintiff's M C P A claim survived in Smith.

The legislature closed that carve out afterward. The current version, M C L four forty five point nine zero four, subsection three, says the act does not apply to, or create a cause of action for, unfair or deceptive practices made unlawful by chapter twenty of the insurance code, for conduct on or after March twenty eighth, two thousand one.
So today, current law bars an M C P A claim against an insurer's claims handling conduct.
And say the reason correctly. Smith is not wrong. It is describing a rule since closed. Those are different criticisms, and only one of them is accurate.
Idea fourteen. Small claims, and two rescission windows.
If you end up in court over a small unpaid balance, know the venue rules.

M C L six hundred point eighty four zero one sets Michigan's small claims jurisdictional limit at seven thousand dollars, effective January first, two thousand twenty four, up from five thousand dollars back in twenty twelve.

M C L six hundred point eighty four zero eight says attorneys cannot participate except on their own behalf. So no lawyers on either side, unless a party removes the case to the general civil division before trial.

Now the last piece, and it is one you touch on nearly every emergency job. Rescission rights on work authorizations signed during a loss. Two different statutes, two different windows, easy to mix up.

The Home Improvement Finance Act, HIFA, applies only when the homeowner is financing the job on installment credit through the contractor, cash price over three hundred dollars. Its rescission window, under M C L four forty five point twelve zero two, is short. Until five p m on the business day following the date of the contract. Call it roughly one business day.

The Home Solicitation Sales Act, HSSA, applies when the contractor solicited the sale at the homeowner's residence. Think a door knocking storm damage salesperson. Its window, under M C L four forty five point one one two, is three business days, running to midnight.
So the pair is: HIFA, financing, five p m the next business day. HSSA, solicited at the door, three business days to midnight. One business day versus three, and five p m versus midnight.
And one important limit on HSSA. A homeowner who calls a contractor herself after a pipe bursts has not been solicited, so HSSA does not automatically apply.
Idea fifteen. The emergency exception, and the handwriting requirement.
HSSA has an emergency exception mitigation companies rely on constantly, and it has three conditions that must all be met.
One, the seller has to, in good faith, substantially begin performance before any cancellation notice.
Two, for goods, they have to be un returnable in substantially as good condition.
And three, critically, the homeowner has to give a separate, dated, signed personal statement, written in her own handwriting, describing the emergency and expressly waiving the three day right.

Read that third one again, because this is where companies fail it. A typed waiver clause at the bottom of the standard work order does not satisfy this. It has to be a separate page, written by hand, by the homeowner.

Skip that step and the homeowner keeps a live cancellation right for three business days, even while the drying equipment is already running in her basement. Think about what that means for your exposure on a job you have already staffed and started.
Question. Storm damage, you knocked on the door, she signs your standard authorization with a typed emergency waiver clause. How long does she have to cancel?

Three business days under HSSA, to midnight. The typed clause does not cut it off, because the exception requires a separate, dated, signed statement in her own handwriting describing the emergency and expressly waiving the right.
Time for the rapid fire recap. Fast, as a self check.

Ninety days to record a construction lien after last furnishing labor or material. One year to foreclose it after recording. Twenty days for a subcontractor's notice of furnishing, zero days for a contractor in direct contract with the owner. Voidable, not void, for an unlicensed contractor's contract with an innocent homeowner, but innocent is doing real legal work, so do not extend it further than the Court did. Post loss assignment of an accrued claim survives an anti assignment clause, back to eighteen eighty, but that protection stops at pre loss transfers. Twelve percent interest belongs to the insured, pursued by the contractor only derivatively. No Michigan Consumer Protection Act claim for chapter twenty insurance conduct after March of two thousand one. Seven thousand dollars is today's small claims ceiling, no lawyers allowed there. One business day to rescind under HIFA, three business days under HSSA, and a handwritten waiver, not a typed one, to cut that HSSA window short in a genuine emergency.

Lock these numbers in, and you will never confuse getting paid for the work with getting to adjust the claim. Two different licenses, two different bodies of law, and confusing them is exactly how a good contractor ends up in front of D I F S.
